messages.text:
I am building an AI pipeline for building international physics olympiad level physics problem sets used for preparing students for competitions. When we build a problem text (PDF) and a solution, we have to evaluate if it the generated solution is correct, and we want to build cost-optimized verifier that suits that kind of problems.

Given the definition of what correct solution means, brainstorm 10 different technical approaches leading from simplest to more complex, to verify if solution is correct for a problem

Don't forget there's a problem first of taking PDF of solution to an ingestible form and that is part of the technical approach brainstorm as well! And don't forget we are not doing grading a solution against a reference solution, the problem is the actual verification of the reference solution!

Read the definition. Here's the brainstorm — ordered simplest → most complex, with the ingestion problem threaded through rather than treated separately.

## First: the ingestion ladder (orthogonal axis)

Every approach below assumes one of these. Pick deliberately — it caps the ceiling of everything downstream.

| | Ingestion | Cost | Loses |
|---|---|---|---|
| **I0** | **Don't ingest the PDF.** Tap the pre-render artifact (LaTeX/MD source + figure source) from your own generator; PDF becomes a rendering-only artifact | ~0 | nothing — but doesn't verify what was *rendered* |
| **I1** | `pymupdf`/`pdftotext` raw text | ~0 | all math structure, figures, layout |
| **I2** | VLM page-images → Markdown+LaTeX transcription | ¢ per page | figure semantics, silent hallucination risk |
| **I3** | I2 + **round-trip check**: re-render transcription to PDF, image-diff / VLM-diff against original; retry on mismatch | 2–3× I2 | little; catches transcription drift |
| **I4** | I3 + **typed semantic IR**: sub-parts, givens with units, equations as SymPy-parseable trees, BCs, asked-quantity + answer-type, figure descriptions, each with a provenance span back to the page | $ | this is the real deliverable |

**The single highest-leverage decision in this whole document is I0.** You control the generator, so you should never be OCR-ing your own output. Keep the PDF path (I3) alive only as a *render-fidelity* check — does the PDF a student sees still say what `S` assumed? That's a genuine V_{P→S} failure channel (a figure that didn't regenerate, an overfull box eating a subscript) and it's the *only* reason to touch the PDF at all.

---

## The 10 approaches

**1. Flat-text single-shot judge** — I1 + one LLM call: "here is P, here is S, is S correct?"
Baseline for the eval harness, not a product. Covers nothing reliably; conflates all three verdicts into one scalar. Its only real job is to be the thing you measure the others against. Expect it to be badly overconfident on faithfulness — the failure mode your definition names as dominant.

**2. Rubric-decomposed judge** — I2 + one call per sub-part, forced to emit the structured multi-axis verdict (V_P / V_S / V_{P→S}, per-condition I–V, first-point-of-failure).
Same intelligence as #1 but the schema does the work: forcing a separate ILL-POSED channel and a separate faithfulness field stops the model from laundering an unfaithful `S` into "looks right." Cheap, ~10× better than #1, and it's the fallback every later tier escalates *to*. Add self-consistency (3 samples, majority) only on disagreement.

**3. Deterministic Tier-0 lint** — I4 + pure code, no LLM at verify time.
SymPy + Pint over the IR: dimensional homogeneity of every equation, units present on every numeric, sig-figs, numeric-in-tolerance, symbol-whitelist compliance, sign/direction fields populated. Runs in milliseconds, costs nothing, and per your §1 empirically catches a large fraction of mechanics faults. The cost isn't here — it's in the LLM pass that builds the IR (#2 gives it to you for free if you make the schema richer). **This is the best cost/benefit item on the list.**

**4. CAS equivalence + plug-back residual** — I4 + SymPy.
Randomized numeric substitution for symbolic equivalence (robust where `simplify()` gives up), approximation-aware via series-expansion-then-compare in the sanctioned small parameter, and EOM-residual: substitute `S`'s answer back into `S`'s *own* governing equations and check ≈0. Note the circularity trap your §5(b) flags — plug-back into self-declared equations certifies nothing if the equations are wrong. It's a falsifier here, not a certifier.

**5. Faithfulness harness as a standalone module** — I4 on *both* P and S, then reconciliation.
Extract two typed fact-tables (givens, geometry, BCs, asked quantities, per sub-part) and do a **bipartite match with an explicit unmatched-residue report**: every datum in P must be used-or-justifiably-ignored by S; every symbol S relies on must trace to P. Mechanically catches the exact generated-content failure your doc calls #1 — a number changed in P but not propagated to S. Mostly deterministic diff once the IR exists; the expensive residue is figure↔prose contradiction, which needs a VLM. Build this early; it has no cheap substitute and it's your dominant risk.

**6. Verifier-as-code-generation** — LLM writes the check, execution renders the verdict.
Per sub-part, the model emits an executable SymPy/NumPy script encoding *the checks it thinks apply* (limiting cases, symmetry, conservation residuals, plug-back). You run it; pass/fail is grounded in execution, not in the model's assertion. Big win: the model is much better at *proposing* a falsifier than at *being* one, and a crashing script is an honest signal. Needs a sandbox and a script-quality gate (a script that trivially passes everything is the failure mode — mutation-test it, see #9).

**7. Independent re-solve and cross-compare (N-version)** — ignore `S`'s reasoning entirely; solve P from scratch k times, compare final forms via #4's CAS equivalence.
This is the only approach so far that attacks **provenance** — right-answer-wrong-reasoning — because agreement on a *derivation-independent* path is evidence the value is physics-forced. Cheap models × many samples beats one expensive sample here. Caveat: correlated errors (all solvers miss the same case split) and it's silent on IPhO problems your solvers simply can't do — which is a meaningful fraction, and you must not read "solver failed" as "S is wrong."

**8. Numerical ground-truth simulation** — build the constraint/ODE model *from P* and integrate it; compare S's closed form against trajectories.
The strongest independent oracle available, and the one that actually adjudicates the things dimensional analysis is blind to: geometric/combinatorial factors, root-branch choice, stick/slip transitions, sign conventions. For the anchor problems this is realistic — finite DOF, standard contact models. Expensive to build (a small library of Lagrangian/contact/hydrostatic templates) and it inherits the Layer-0 risk: a wrong constraint inventory produces a simulation that confidently disagrees with a correct `S`. Use it where Tier 1 is silent — dimensionless answers especially.

**9. Adversarial pairing + mutation-calibrated cascade** — a refuter agent whose *only* goal is to produce a concrete falsifying instance (a limiting case where S breaks, a case split S skipped), paired against a defender, with escalation triggers from §5.
The critical piece here isn't the debate, it's the **mutation harness**: systematically inject faults into known-good anchor solutions — flip a sign, drop a factor of 2, change a datum in P but not S, delete a case branch — and measure per-tier catch rate. That's how you learn what your cascade's actual false-accept rate is, and it's how you stop #6's scripts and #2's rubric from degenerating into rubber stamps. Do this even if you build nothing else from this row.

**10. Proof-carrying solutions** — change the *generator*, not the verifier.
Require `S` to be emitted in a typed physics DSL: each step is a named inference (apply Newton II in frame F, integrate with BC B, expand to O(ε²)) over dimensioned quantities, with the prose PDF rendered *from* the DSL. Verification becomes step-by-step mechanical checking — dimensional types check by construction, each rewrite is CAS-verifiable, case coverage is a totality check on the branch structure. Highest ceiling: it's the only approach that gives real provenance and real derivational validity rather than endpoint checks. Also the highest cost, and it constrains what the generator can express — worth prototyping on the 2020 Anisotropic Friction anchor before committing.

---

## What I'd actually build

**I0 ingestion → #2's IR extraction → #3 + #4 deterministic core → #5 faithfulness module → #9's mutation harness to calibrate**, with #2 as the escalation target and #8 reserved for dimensionless/geometric-factor answers.

That's roughly your Layer 0/1 with the expensive parts deferred. #7 and #10 are the two genuinely different bets — #7 buys provenance cheaply but noisily, #10 buys it expensively but soundly. I'd resolve open-decision §8.2 (run Layer 1 against the anchors) before choosing between them, since the answer depends on what fraction of sub-parts the cheap core actually adjudicates.

## First, your questions

**I4 vs I2/I3 cost — you're right, it's empirical, and it's cheap to settle.** My "cents → dollars" was hand-waving. The real variable is retry rate: if IPhO solution PDFs transcribe cleanly in one VLM pass, I4 costs barely more than I2 (same image tokens in, a richer schema out — maybe 2× the output tokens). If they need 2–3 round-trips because of dense math and figures, it's 3×. **Run this on the 6 anchor PDFs before anything else** — it's ~$5 of API spend and it pins down the input cost for all four systems below. I'd bet on I4 being cheap, because you're paying image-token cost either way and the marginal cost of a richer schema is output tokens only.

**"Lint alone would degrade quality insanely" — correct, and I mis-framed it.** The deterministic lint is not a *system*, it's a *layer*. It never connects P's physical model to S's — it can't, it has no semantics. It only refutes. It appears inside all four systems below as a free pre-filter; it is never one of them. What I should have said: it's the best cost/benefit *component*, contingent on the IR the LLM already produced.

**CAS is ~$0 marginal given I4 — yes, with one caveat.** Compute is free. But "sanctioned approximation" handling isn't purely mechanical: deciding *which* small parameter to expand in and to what order is a judgment call the IR extraction has to carry. So it's $0 of new spend but it adds requirements to the extraction schema. Fold it in.

**#6 code-gen is the expensive/high-quality end — agreed, that's S4.**

**#7 N-version re-solve — agreed, later.**

**#9 — partly disagree.** The *debate agent* is a later experiment, yes. But the **mutation harness is eval infrastructure, not a verifier tier**, and you need it from day 1 for exactly the reason you named: you can't tell whether your definition of correctness is right until you can measure false-accept rate on known-bad solutions. It costs nothing at inference time. Build it alongside S3.

---

## Five prompt-engineering directions for the rubric judge

1. **Answer-type routing.** Your §1.4 says answers cluster into ~6 pre-declarable forms. Make type selection a separate cheap call, then dispatch to a *type-specific* judge prompt. A "show-that" checker and a "graph feature list" checker share almost no rubric. This kills your §7.6 failure mode (mis-typing silently applies a weaker test) by making the type an explicit, auditable decision rather than an implicit one.

2. **Schema-as-CoT.** Instead of "think step by step then answer," force a structured output whose *field order* is the reasoning order: `governing_law_identified → regime_assumed → dimensional_check → case_branches_found → first_point_of_failure → verdict`. The schema does the decomposition, and every field is independently inspectable when the verdict is wrong. Much better than free-form CoT for a reward signal.

3. **Extract-then-adjudicate split.** Two calls: one produces the IR from S, one judges the IR against P. If they're the same call, the model launders its own extraction errors into the verdict — it reads what it expected to read and then confirms it. Splitting makes extraction faults visible as IR faults.

4. **Refuter framing.** "Produce one concrete falsifying instance — a limiting case where this breaks, a case split it skipped, a datum it ignored — or state that you failed to find one" beats "is this correct?" Models are far better at generating a counterexample than at rendering a global verdict. Default the frame to *refuted unless you failed to refute*.

5. **Mutation-derived few-shots.** Once #9's harness exists, your injected faults become the exemplar set: here's a sign flip, here's a dropped factor of 2, here's a missed stick/slip branch. Real in-distribution negatives, not synthetic ones. This is the highest-leverage prompt change available and it's free once the harness exists.

*(Bonus, which is really a cost lever: lay the prompt out **stable-first** — P and S at the front, the sub-part question at the very end. This is what makes prefix caching work across 12 sub-part calls, and it's worth ~3× on the judge tier. See below.)*

---

## The four systems

Costed per problem verified. Assumptions: ~12 sub-parts; P ≈ 4k tokens and S ≈ 12k tokens after ingestion; ~11 PDF pages ≈ 18k image tokens. Pricing: Opus 4.8 `$5/$25` per MTok, Sonnet 5 `$3/$15` (intro `$2/$10` through 2026-08-31), Haiku 4.5 `$1/$5`; cache reads ~0.1×, cache writes 1.25×; Batch API 50% off. **These are order-of-magnitude, not quotes** — the ingestion experiment above moves the first line item.

### S4 — Agentic verifier, per-sub-part tool loop — **~$8**

I4 ingestion with round-trip verification. Per sub-part, an Opus agent with a SymPy/NumPy sandbox writes and runs its own checks — dimensional, limiting-case, conservation residual, plug-back — then adjudicates on execution results. Findings go to a 3-vote adversarial refuter panel.

- Ingestion (I4 + round-trip): ~$0.70
- 12 × agent loop (~5 turns, ~60k cumulative in / 8k out): ~$6.00
- Adversarial verify on ~4 flagged sub-parts × 3 votes: ~$1.20

**What you get:** the model builds a verifier optimized per problem, and every pass/fail is grounded in execution rather than assertion. Best quality and, as you said, the best early-eval signal — it tells you *what checks the problem actually needed*, which is information the other three can't produce. **What you pay for:** a sandbox, a script-quality gate, and 4× S3's cost.

### S3 — Structured cascade with escalation — **~$3.60**

I4 ingestion → deterministic Tier-0 (SymPy + Pint + CAS equivalence + plug-back, $0) → per-sub-part Opus rubric judge using techniques 1/2/4 above → escalate ~25% of sub-parts (dimensionless answers, Tier-0 disagreement, qualitative deliverables) to an S4-style agent.

- Ingestion: ~$0.48
- 12 × Opus judge (17k in / 2k out): ~$1.62
- 3 × escalated agent runs: ~$1.50

**This is the natural V1.** It has the full architecture; the escalation tier is where the expensive intelligence lives, and it fires only where the cheap layer is provably silent.

### S2 — S3 with the free levers pulled — **~$1.76 (51% of S3)**

Same architecture, same escalation logic. Three changes, none architectural:

- **Prefix caching.** Lay out P+S once, ask 12 sub-part questions against the cached prefix. First call writes (1.25×), eleven read at 0.1×.
- **Sonnet 5 for the judge tier**, Opus reserved for escalation only.
- **Sonnet for ingestion transcription**, Opus only for the IR structuring pass if the round-trip check fails.

- Ingestion: ~$0.29
- Judge tier: ~$0.47 ← *was $1.62*
- Escalation (Opus, ~2 sub-parts): ~$1.00

**The point of this row:** the judge tier collapses 3.4× and I have *not* removed a single check. Caching alone is most of it — 12 calls that each re-read a 16k prefix at full price is pure waste, and fixing it costs one prompt reordering. The Sonnet swap is the only quality-bearing change, and it's on the tier where a wrong answer escalates anyway.

### S1 — Single-pass, no escalation — **~$0.55 (31% of S2)**

I2 ingestion (no round-trip, no full IR — so no deterministic layer). One Sonnet pass per sub-part with the rubric schema, submitted through the Batch API at 50% off. No escalation tier, no adversarial pass.

- Ingestion: ~$0.18
- Batched judge tier: ~$0.30
- Escalation: $0

**What you lost:** everything in §5's Tier-2 trigger list. Dimensionless/geometric-factor answers, qualitative deliverables, and Tier-0/Tier-1 disagreements now get the *same* treatment as a clean symbolic answer. Per your own §6, that's the highest residual risk in the whole spec. Plus batch latency (minutes to an hour), which is fine for offline generation and fatal for interactive.

---

## What "half cost" actually means here

That's the thing worth taking away:

| Step | Factor | What it cost you in quality |
|---|---|---|
| S4 → S3 | 2.2× | Agentic checks only where triggered, not everywhere. Real but bounded loss. |
| S3 → S2 | 2.0× | **Almost nothing.** Caching is free; the Sonnet swap is on a tier that escalates on doubt. |
| S2 → S1 | 3.2× | The entire expert residue. This is where you start eating your definition. |

The first 50% is an engineering artifact, not a tradeoff — you're currently paying for it by re-sending the same 16k prefix twelve times. The second 50% is where you delete Layer 2. So the useful question isn't "can we halve cost" (yes, twice, easily) but **"how far down the ladder can we go before false-accept rate on the mutation set moves?"** — and that's unanswerable until the harness exists.

Concretely, I'd build **S3, instrument it with the mutation harness, then measure S2 and S1 against the same fault set.** If S2 catches the same faults as S3, ship S2 and put the savings into S4-style escalation on the sub-parts that actually need it.

**What changed materially from the Claude version of this analysis** — and it sharpens the conclusion rather than just rescaling it:

On OpenAI's pricing, twelve fully-cached `luna` sub-part judgments cost **$0.18**. Two `sol` agent runs cost **$0.68**. So in S2, the escalation tier is 70% of total cost while adjudicating 2 of 12 sub-parts. The bulk judging tier has essentially collapsed to a rounding error — which means the cost question is no longer "which model do we use" but **"how many sub-parts escalate, and can we predict which ones cheaply?"** Tightening the escalation trigger by one sub-part saves more than moving the entire bulk tier from `terra` all the way down to `nano`.

**Two things in the doc I flagged rather than asserted:**

- **Reasoning tokens bill as output.** Every output estimate therefore includes reasoning spend, and reasoning effort is a cost lever on par with model choice. These are the least certain numbers in the file — the agent-loop figures especially.

Steps are now 2.2× / 2.0× / 3.2× — the middle two are clean halvings, which is a tidier ladder than before. The headline finding softens but survives: escalation drops from 70% to **54%** of S2's cost while still handling only ~2 of 12 sub-parts. One new consequence I added — because escalation is now cheap, the trigger can afford to be *generous*, so widening it is the cheapest quality gain available if recall turns out to be trigger-limited.

**One thing I flagged rather than just applying.** Capping at `terra` halves the dominant line item, but escalation is precisely where DEFINITION.MD §3 puts the irreducible expert core — faithfulness, law-applicability, non-menu case completeness, provenance. Those are the judgments most likely to be capability-limited rather than prompt-limited, so it's the one place where the model tier might genuinely matter. I wrote it into §0 as an explicit unvalidated bet with a test attached: run a `sol` escalation arm in the harness. If both tiers catch the same injected faults the saving is free; if `sol` catches more, ~2× on a tier that touches 2 of 12 sub-parts is probably worth paying. Cheap to check, and better to know than to assume.

**Experiment inputs** are now a named §6 with the exact paths — `pdfs/IPhO_2021_S1.pdf` (must PASS) against `pdfs/faulty/IPhO_2021_S1_FAULTY.pdf` (must FAIL), with `IPhO_2021_Q1.pdf` as the problem statement. Two notes worth surfacing:

- I made the clean/faulty framing explicit as **false-reject vs. false-accept**. The faulty file gives you §8.2's number, but the clean file matters just as much — a verifier that rejects a genuine IPhO reference solution is unusable no matter what else it catches.
- I found `IPhO_2023_S3_FAULTY.pdf` in the same directory and wrote it up as a **held-out** second pair. Recommend not tuning prompts against it; after you iterate on 2021 it's your only uncontaminated read on whether the tuning generalized.
